lessons.title: The staff and the treble clef
lessons.summary: Read the nine notes on the staff and play them in open position.
body: ## Five lines, four spaces

Music is written on a staff of five lines. Every line and every space stands for one letter name. Each step up, from a line to the next space or from a space to the next line, moves up one letter: A B C D E F G, then A again.
## The treble clef
The sign at the start of the staff is the treble clef, also called the G clef. Its inner curl circles the second line from the bottom, and that line is G.
- Lines, bottom to top: E G B D F
- Spaces, bottom to top: F A C E
## Guitar sounds an octave lower

Guitar music is written in treble clef but sounds one octave lower than written. That is the small 8 under the clef. The bottom line E is the E on the 4th string, 2nd fret, and that is the pitch the app listens for when you answer by playing.
## How to practise

Say each name out loud. Do not count up from the bottom line every time: learn landmarks. Bottom line E, middle line B, top line F, and the four spaces spell FACE. Then answer by clicking, and after that by playing each note on the guitar.

lessons.title: Notes on the neck
lessons.summary: Find the natural notes on every string, starting with the 6th and 5th.
body: ## Open strings
From the thickest string to the thinnest: E A D G B E. The 6th string is the low E and the 1st string is the high E, two octaves higher.
## One fret is one half step
Moving up one fret raises the note by one half step (one semitone). Most natural notes are two frets apart, except E to F and B to C, which are only one fret apart.
- 6th string: E 0, F 1, G 3, A 5, B 7, C 8, D 10, E 12
- 5th string: A 0, B 2, C 3, D 5, E 7, F 8, G 10, A 12
## Landmarks
- Fret 12 is the open string one octave higher. The fret markers at 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12 are your signposts.
- Fret 5 on one string gives the next higher open string, except on the 3rd (G) string, where it is fret 4.
- The same letter appears two strings higher and two frets higher (the octave shape), on the 6th to 4th and 5th to 3rd strings.
## Open position on the staff

Notes below the staff are written with short extra lines called ledger lines. The open low E is written below three ledger lines. In open position every natural note from low E up to G on the 1st string, 3rd fret, can be played within the first three frets.

exercises.title: Play open position from the staff

lessons.title: Half steps, whole steps, sharps and flats
lessons.summary: Measure in semitones and tones, and name the notes between the naturals.
body: ## Semitones and tones

A half step, also called a semitone, is the smallest distance in Western music: one fret on the guitar. A whole step, also called a tone, is two half steps: two frets. In this course distances are always given both ways, so 3 semitones is the same as 1½ tones.
## Sharps and flats
A sharp (♯) raises a note by one half step, one fret higher. A flat (♭) lowers it by one half step, one fret lower. A natural sign (♮) cancels a sharp or flat.
The note between F and G can be called F♯ or G♭: the same fret, two names. Notes like this are called enharmonic. There is no note between E and F, or between B and C.
## The chromatic scale

All twelve notes in a row, one fret apart, make the chromatic scale: C C♯ D D♯ E F F♯ G G♯ A A♯ B C, or with flats: C D♭ D E♭ E F G♭ G A♭ A B♭ B C. Play it up the 6th string from the open E to the 12th fret and say each name.
## On the staff
The sharp or flat is written just before the note head, on the same line or space. It lasts until the end of the bar.

exercises.title: Name it with sharps and flats

lessons.title: Intervals: semitones and tones from the root
lessons.summary: Name the 13 intervals in an octave by sound, by shape and by distance.
body: ## What an interval is

An interval is the distance between two notes. It has a number and a quality. The number comes from counting letter names, counting both ends: C up to E is C D E, a 3rd. The quality (perfect, major, minor, augmented, diminished) comes from the exact number of semitones.
## The intervals in one octave
- 0 semitones · 0 tones · unison (P1)
- 1 · ½ · minor 2nd (m2)
- 2 · 1 · major 2nd (M2)
- 3 · 1½ · minor 3rd (m3)
- 4 · 2 · major 3rd (M3)
- 5 · 2½ · perfect 4th (P4)
- 6 · 3 · tritone (A4 or d5)
- 7 · 3½ · perfect 5th (P5)
- 8 · 4 · minor 6th (m6)
- 9 · 4½ · major 6th (M6)
- 10 · 5 · minor 7th (m7)
- 11 · 5½ · major 7th (M7)
- 12 · 6 · octave (P8)
## On the guitar

On one string, the number of frets is the number of semitones. Across strings: the same fret on the next higher string is a perfect 4th, except from the 3rd (G) to the 2nd (B) string, where it is a major 3rd. Two frets up on the next string is a perfect 5th, the power-chord shape.
## By ear
Sing the lower note, then the upper one. Major 3rds sound bright, minor 3rds darker, perfect 4ths and 5ths open and hollow, the tritone tense, and the octave like the same note higher.

lessons.title: The major scale
lessons.summary: Build any major scale from its step pattern, and play it in one octave.
body: ## One pattern, twelve keys

A major scale is seven notes, one for each letter name, followed by the first note an octave higher. What makes it major is the distance between neighbours: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half (W W H W W W H). In semitones that is 2 2 1 2 2 2 1.
Start on C and the pattern lands only on natural notes: C D E F G A B C. Start anywhere else and you need sharps or flats to keep the pattern.
## Building a scale
- Write the seven letters in order from the root: G A B C D E F G.
- Walk the pattern and fix each note with a sharp or flat. G to A is W, A to B is W, B to C is H, C to D is W, D to E is W, E to F must be W, so F becomes F♯, and F♯ to G is H.
- Every letter appears once. That is why D major uses F♯ and not G♭: G is already taken by the 4th note.
## Degrees

The notes are numbered 1 to 7 from the root. Musicians talk in these numbers all the time ("play the 3rd", "the 5th of the key"), and so does Gleason's book. In D major: 1 D, 2 E, 3 F♯, 4 G, 5 A, 6 B, 7 C♯.
## On the guitar

On one string the pattern is frets: 0 2 4 5 7 9 11 12. Across the neck, a one-octave shape starting with the 2nd finger on the 6th string covers the whole scale without moving your hand. The Practice tab shows all five positions.

exercises.title: Spell major scales: C G D F B♭
Play the scale you are given

lessons.title: Key signatures and the circle of fifths
lessons.summary: Read a key signature at a glance and find any key on the circle.
body: ## Key signatures

Writing F♯ every time in G major gets old, so the sharps or flats of the key are written once at the start of every line: the key signature. A sharp on the top line means every F is F♯, in every octave, unless a natural sign says otherwise.
## Always in the same order
- Sharps: F C G D A E B (Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle)
- Flats: B E A D G C F (the same words backwards)
- Sharp keys: the key is a half step above the last sharp. Three sharps end on G♯, so the key is A major.
- Flat keys: the key is the second-to-last flat. Three flats (B♭ E♭ A♭): E♭ major. One flat is F major; learn that one by heart.
## The circle of fifths

Put the twelve keys around a clock face, C at the top. Each step clockwise goes up a perfect 5th and adds one sharp: C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯. Each step counter-clockwise goes up a perfect 4th and adds one flat: C, F, B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭. At the bottom, F♯ and G♭ are the same keys spelled two ways.

Neighbours on the circle share six of their seven notes, which is why songs move so easily between them. The I, IV and V chords of any key (the three chords of the blues) sit right next to each other: IV is one step counter-clockwise, V one step clockwise.
## On the guitar

The circle is also a fingerboard shape: the same fret on the next string up is a 4th higher, one step counter-clockwise. The same fret on the next string down is a 4th lower, which is the same letter as a 5th up: one step clockwise. Moving a shape across the strings walks you around the circle.

exercises.title: Name the major key: up to 4 sharps or flats
Name the major key: all keys

lessons.title: Minor scales and relative keys
lessons.summary: Natural and harmonic minor, and the major key that shares each minor key's notes.
body: ## Natural minor

Play the notes of C major but start and end on A: A B C D E F G A. That is A natural minor. Its step pattern is W H W W H W W. Compared with A major it has a lowered 3rd, 6th and 7th: 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7.
## Relative keys

A minor and C major use the same seven notes and the same key signature: they are relative keys. Every major key has a relative minor three semitones (a minor 3rd) below it: G major and E minor, F major and D minor, E♭ major and C minor.
- From a major key to its relative minor: down 3 semitones, or up to the 6th degree.
- From a minor key to its relative major: up 3 semitones, the ♭3.
On the circle of fifths each minor key sits next to its relative major.
## Harmonic minor

Raise the 7th of natural minor by a half step: A B C D E F G♯ A. The gap between F and G♯ is a step and a half (3 semitones), which gives the scale its exotic sound. The raised 7th, the leading tone, pulls strongly up to the root, and it turns the V chord into a major chord: E major instead of E minor in A minor.
## Melodic minor
Jazz players use melodic minor: natural minor with both the 6th and 7th raised, A B C D E F♯ G♯ A, the same going up and down. You will meet it again before Gleason; for now just know it exists.
## Hearing the difference
Major sounds settled and bright. Natural minor sounds darker and sadder. Harmonic minor has that one wide step near the top. Listen for the 3rd first, then the step into the octave.

exercises.title: Ear: major, natural or harmonic minor?

lessons.title: Triads: major, minor, diminished, augmented
lessons.summary: Stack two 3rds to make the four kinds of triad, and hear the difference.
body: ## Stacking 3rds
A triad is three notes stacked in 3rds: a root, the 3rd above it and the 5th above it. On the staff a root-position triad looks like a snowman: three notes on three lines or three spaces in a row.
## Four kinds
- Major: major 3rd + minor 3rd, so root, 3, 5. C E G. Symbol: C.
- Minor: minor 3rd + major 3rd, so root, ♭3, 5. C E♭ G. Symbol: Cm.
- Diminished: minor 3rd + minor 3rd, so root, ♭3, ♭5. C E♭ G♭. Symbol: C°.
- Augmented: major 3rd + major 3rd, so root, 3, ♯5. C E G♯. Symbol: C+.
Major and minor triads have a perfect 5th from root to top (7 semitones). Diminished squeezes it to 6, augmented stretches it to 8.
## Where they come from

Build a triad on every note of the major scale using only notes of the scale and you get, in order: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished. In C: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°. This is the harmony of the key, and you will use it constantly from Level 3 on.
## By ear
Major sounds bright and stable, minor darker. Diminished is tense and wants to move. Augmented sounds unresolved and dreamy, as if it is floating.

exercises.title: Name the triad on the staff
Play the triad, note by note

lessons.title: Triad inversions on string sets
lessons.summary: Three ways to stack every triad, on three adjacent strings all over the neck.
body: ## Inversions
The notes of a triad can be stacked in any order. Which note is lowest, the bass, gives the inversion:
- Root position: the root is in the bass. C E G.
- 1st inversion: the 3rd is in the bass. E G C.
- 2nd inversion: the 5th is in the bass. G C E.
Each inversion still has all three notes, so it is still a C major chord, but it sounds a little different and lies in a different place on the neck.
## On three strings

Put one note on each of three neighbouring strings (1-2-3, 2-3-4, 3-4-5 or 4-5-6) and every triad has three small shapes, one per inversion. Walking up one string set, the shapes follow each other in a cycle: root position, 1st inversion, 2nd inversion, root position an octave higher.
These small shapes are what Gleason calls triad shapes and uses for comping and soloing. Learn them on strings 1-2-3 first, the most useful set, then 2-3-4.
## How to practise

Pick a chord. Find its three shapes on strings 1-2-3 from the lowest fret up and say the bass note of each: the root, the 3rd or the 5th. Then change major to minor by lowering the 3rd one fret, wherever it is.

lessons.title: Interval shapes on the neck
lessons.summary: See every interval as a shape you can move anywhere, including the B-string shift.
body: ## Shapes, not counting

Because the guitar is tuned in 4ths (with one exception), every interval has the same shape wherever you play it. Learn the shape once and you can find a 3rd, a 5th or an octave from any note without thinking of note names.
## From a root on the 6th, 5th or 4th string
- Next string, same fret: perfect 4th.
- Next string, 2 frets up: perfect 5th (the power chord).
- Next string, 1 fret down: major 3rd. 2 frets down: minor 3rd.
- Two strings up, 2 frets up: octave.
- Two strings up, same fret: minor 7th. 1 fret up: major 7th.
- Two strings up, 1 fret down: major 6th. 2 frets down: minor 6th.
## The B-string shift

The G and B strings are a major 3rd apart, not a 4th. Any shape that crosses from the 3rd string to the 2nd moves one fret higher on the B string and above. The octave from the 4th string is 3 frets up, not 2; from the 3rd string it is 3 frets up, two strings over.
## How to practise
Name the shape before you name the notes. Then play each interval from a root on every string, saying its name and its size: "perfect 5th, 7 semitones, 3½ tones".

exercises.title: Play the interval from any root

lessons.title: Seventh chords
lessons.summary: Add one more 3rd on top of a triad: the five seventh chords of jazz and blues.
body: ## Four notes
Stack one more 3rd on a triad and you get a seventh chord: root, 3rd, 5th and 7th. Almost every chord in jazz, and in Gleason's book, is a seventh chord.
## The five types
- Major 7th (Cmaj7): major triad + major 7th. C E G B. Smooth and dreamy.
- Dominant 7th (C7): major triad + minor 7th. C E G B♭. Bluesy and restless; it wants to move.
- Minor 7th (Cm7): minor triad + minor 7th. C E♭ G B♭. Soft and mellow.
- Half-diminished (Cm7♭5, also Cø): diminished triad + minor 7th. C E♭ G♭ B♭. Dark, leading somewhere.
- Diminished 7th (C°7): diminished triad + diminished 7th. C E♭ G♭ B♭♭ (sounds like A). Very tense and symmetrical: every note is a minor 3rd apart.
## Telling them apart

Look at the triad first (major, minor or diminished), then the 7th: a major 7th is one fret below the octave, a minor 7th two frets below. Major triad + minor 7th is the dominant, the one used for blues.
## By ear

Major 7th has a soft rub between the 7th and the octave. Dominant 7th sounds like the blues. Minor 7th is calm and warm. Half-diminished is darker than minor 7th, as if the floor has dropped a little.

exercises.title: Name the seventh chord on the staff

lessons.title: The chords of a key and Roman numerals
lessons.summary: Build a triad on every note of the major scale and name it by its number.
body: ## Chords from the scale
Build a triad on each note of a major scale, using only notes of that scale: skip one note, take one, skip one, take one. In C: C E G, D F A, E G B, F A C, G B D, A C E, B D F.
## Always the same pattern
In every major key the qualities come out in the same order: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished. Learn this once and you know the chords of all twelve keys.
## Roman numerals
Chords are named by the degree they are built on, in Roman numerals: capitals for major, lower case for minor, a small circle for diminished.
- I ii iii IV V vi vii°
- In C: C Dm Em F G Am B°
- In G: G Am Bm C D Em F♯°
This is the thinking in numbers that runs all the way through Gleason's book: a song that goes I vi IV V is the same song in any key.
## On the guitar

Play the seven chords of G major with open and barre chords, saying the numerals out loud: one, two minor, three minor, four, five, six minor. Leave out the vii° for now; it is mostly used as a seventh chord or as part of the V7.

exercises.title: Chords of C, G and F

lessons.title: Diatonic seventh chords and what they do
lessons.summary: The seven 7th chords of a key, and the three jobs a chord can do.
body: ## Seventh chords from the scale
Stack one more 3rd and each chord of the key becomes a seventh chord. The pattern is again the same in every key:
- Imaj7  IIm7  IIIm7  IVmaj7  V7  VIm7  VIIm7♭5
- In C: Cmaj7 Dm7 Em7 Fmaj7 G7 Am7 Bm7♭5
Only one chord of the key is a dominant 7th: the V7. That is why a dominant 7th tells the ear where home is. (The blues breaks this rule on purpose and makes every chord a dominant.)
## Three jobs
- Tonic (home, at rest): I, and also iii and vi, which share two notes with it.
- Subdominant (moving away): IV and ii.
- Dominant (tension that wants to go home): V and vii. They contain the 7th degree of the scale, which pulls up to the root, and the tritone between the 4th and the 7th.
Most music moves tonic, subdominant, dominant, tonic: away from home, a build-up of tension, and back.
## Hearing it
Play I, IV, V7 and stop. The music feels unfinished. Play the I again and it resolves. That pull of V7 to I is the strongest force in Western harmony.

exercises.title: Ear: all four diatonic 7th chord types

lessons.title: Progressions and the II-V-I
lessons.summary: The chord sequences behind thousands of songs, and the most important one in jazz.
body: ## Progressions by number
A chord progression is a sequence of chords. Written in numerals it fits every key.
- I IV V I: folk, rock and roll, country.
- I vi IV V: the 1950s doo-wop progression.
- I V vi IV: a huge number of pop songs.
- vi IV I V: the same chords starting from the minor one.
## II-V-I

IIm7 V7 Imaj7 is the backbone of jazz. The roots move up a 4th each time (D to G to C in C major), the strongest root movement there is. Gleason's harmony chapters, and most jazz standards, are built from chains of II-V-Is in different keys.
## Guide tones

In a II-V-I the 7th of each chord moves down a half step to the 3rd of the next: C (7th of Dm7) to B (3rd of G7), F (7th of G7) to E (3rd of Cmaj7). Play only those notes and you can hear the whole progression in two voices.
## By ear
Follow the bass. From the I, a move up a 4th (to IV) sounds open; a move up a 5th (to V) sounds like a question; a move down to the vi sounds like a sigh into minor.

lessons.title: Reading rhythm
lessons.summary: Note values, counting out loud, dotted notes and syncopation, tapped in time.
body: ## Note values
In 4/4 time there are four beats in a bar and a quarter note lasts one beat. A half note lasts 2, a whole note 4, an eighth note ½ and a sixteenth ¼. Rests are silences of the same lengths.
## Counting

Count the beats as numbers and the halves of each beat as "and": 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &. Eighth notes fall on numbers and ands; quarter notes only on numbers. Always count out loud, at least in your head, while you read.
## Dots and syncopation
- A dot adds half the value again: a dotted half is 3 beats, a dotted quarter 1½. A dotted quarter followed by an eighth is a very common pattern: 1 - - & .
- Syncopation puts notes on the ands instead of the beats. Eighth, quarter, eighth is counted 1 & - &: the middle note starts on the "and" of 1 and lasts across beat 2.
## How to tap

Press Start: you hear four clicks, then the click goes on through the rhythm. Tap each note as it starts, with the pad, the Space bar, or by strumming muted strings on the guitar (the app hears the attack). Only the start of each note matters; how long it lasts does not.

lessons.title: Sixteenths, triplets and rhythm cells
lessons.summary: Split the beat in three or four, and learn the cells as words you can say and play.
body: ## Three or four pulses

Every beat can be split into four sixteenths (1 e & a) or into three triplet eighths (1 trip let). Playing some of those pulses and not others gives a small rhythm cell. Most rhythms are just cells strung together, so learn them as units, like words.
## Three-pulse cells
- Triplet: all three (1 trip let).
- Swing: the first and the last (1 - let). This is the shuffle and swing feel.
- Afro-Cuban: the first two (1 trip -).
- Waltz: the last two (- trip let).
These four names come from Gleason's book, which calls rhythm cells rhythmic words.
## Four-pulse cells
- All four (1 e & a): four sixteenths.
- 1 - & -: two eighths.
- 1 - & a: an eighth and two sixteenths.
- 1 e & -: two sixteenths and an eighth.
- 1 - - a: a dotted eighth and a sixteenth.
Gleason gives the four-pulse cells names too (gallop, jingle bells, Creedence and others). When you reach his rhythmic words chapter, match each of his names to one of these syllable patterns.
## How to practise
Gleason's method: strum the cell in the air while you say it, then clap it while counting, then play it on one note. Say the syllables out loud every time.

lessons.title: The 12-bar blues
lessons.summary: Three chords, twelve bars: the form under almost every blues.
body: ## Twelve bars, three chords
A blues chorus is 12 bars of 4 beats. It uses three chords built on the 1st, 4th and 5th notes of the key: the I, IV and V. In A they are A, D and E; in E they are E, A and B.
- Bars 1-4: I I I I (the statement)
- Bars 5-8: IV IV I I (the answer)
- Bars 9-12: V IV I V (the punchline and the turnaround)
The last bar, the V, is the turnaround: it pulls back to bar 1 for the next chorus. Songs repeat this chorus again and again, with a sung line in each group of four bars.
## Dominant 7th chords

In blues, all three chords are usually dominant 7th chords: a major triad with a minor 7th on top. A7 is A C♯ E G: root, 3, 5, ♭7. The ♭7 gives the rough, unresolved sound of the blues, and in a blues it never needs to resolve.
## Think in numbers

Learn the form as numbers, not chord names. Then you can play it in any key: find the I, count up the major scale to 4 and 5. On the guitar the IV is the same fret one string higher, and the V is two frets above that.
## Listen for it
Put on any blues and count the bars out loud. The change to the IV in bar 5 is easy to hear: the bass goes up a 4th and the music opens up. The V in bar 9 is the most tense moment of the chorus.

exercises.title: Which chord is in that bar?
I, IV and V in any key
Ear: I to IV or I to V?

lessons.title: Shuffle, straight, slow and funk
lessons.summary: The same 12 bars feel completely different with a different groove.
body: ## Shuffle

Most blues swings. Each beat is split in three, like a triplet, and the eighth notes fall on the first and third parts: a long note and a short one, da-ga da-ga. Say "Hump-ty Dump-ty". This is the shuffle, and when you play eighth notes over it, play them long-short too.
## Straight
In a straight feel (rock and roll, Chuck Berry style) each beat is split in two equal halves: one-and two-and. The same licks sound harder and more driving.
## Slow blues
Slow blues counts four slow beats per bar, each split in three: 12 pulses per bar, written in 12/8. There is lots of space, so every note counts: bend slowly, use vibrato, and leave gaps.
## Funk
Funk blues splits the beat in four (sixteenth notes) and the bass plays a busy, syncopated riff. Short, percussive notes work best.
## How to practise
In the Backing tracks tab, play the same 12 bars in each feel, at a slow tempo, and just play the root of each chord in time. Then play one lick over each feel and hear how its rhythm has to change.

lessons.title: Minor pentatonic, box 1
lessons.summary: Five notes that work over the whole blues, in the shape everyone starts with.
body: ## Five notes

The minor pentatonic scale has five notes: 1, ♭3, 4, 5, ♭7. In A: A C D E G. Leave out the 2nd and 6th of natural minor and nothing is left that can clash, which is why it works over all three chords of a blues.
## Box 1

Put your index finger on the root on the 6th string (fret 5 for A, fret 12 or 0 for E). Box 1 is two notes on every string, within four frets: index finger and ring finger on most strings, index and pinky where the notes are three frets apart.
- 6th string: 1 and ♭3
- 5th string: 4 and 5
- 4th string: ♭7 and 1
- 3rd string: ♭3 and 4
- 2nd string: 5 and ♭7
- 1st string: 1 and ♭3
There are three roots in the box: 6th string, 4th string and 1st string. Always know where they are; phrases sound finished when they end on one.
## How to practise

Play the box up and down with the metronome (Practice > Scales, minor pentatonic, Box 1). Say the degree of each note out loud. Then improvise over a backing track using only the 4th and 3rd strings: four notes are enough to make music.

lessons.title: The blues scale and the blue note
lessons.summary: Add the ♭5 to the minor pentatonic and you have the blues scale.
body: ## One extra note
The blues scale is the minor pentatonic with one note added between the 4 and the 5: the ♭5, also called the blue note. In A: A C D E♭ E G.
## How to use it

The ♭5 is tense and sour on its own. Use it as a passing note, on the way from the 4 to the 5 or back, or as a quick hammer-on and pull-off. Sitting on it for long sounds wrong; brushing past it sounds like the blues.
## Where it is
In box 1 the blue note is on the 5th string, one fret above the 4, and on the 3rd string, one fret above the 4 again. Those two places give you most of the classic blues-scale licks.
## Blue notes in general
Singers and guitarists bend many notes a little: the ♭3 towards the 3, the ♭7 towards the 7, the ♭5 towards the 5. These in-between pitches are what makes blues sound vocal. Lesson 6 covers bends.

exercises.title: Ear: minor pentatonic or blues scale?

lessons.title: Five boxes across the neck
lessons.summary: Link the five pentatonic shapes so the whole neck is yours.
body: ## Five shapes, one scale

The five notes of the minor pentatonic repeat all over the neck. Starting each shape from the next note of the scale on the 6th string gives five boxes. Box 1 starts on the root, box 2 on the ♭3, box 3 on the 4, box 4 on the 5 and box 5 on the ♭7. After box 5 comes box 1 again, an octave higher.
## They overlap

The top of each box is the bottom of the next one: the notes on the right edge of box 1 are the notes on the left edge of box 2. Learn the boxes in pairs, 1 and 2, then 2 and 3, and slide between them on one string.
## Find the roots
Every box has two or three roots. Find them first in each box (the gold dots on the diagram), then the rest of the shape hangs around them.
## Same shapes, other keys
The boxes never change shape. Moving to another key just slides them all up or down the neck: in A box 1 is at fret 5, in C at fret 8, in E at fret 0 or 12.

exercises.title: Degrees in the blues scale boxes
Play the scale in any box

lessons.title: Bends, slides, vibrato and phrasing
lessons.summary: How to make five notes talk: expressive technique and call and response.
body: ## Bends

Push the string across the fret to raise its pitch. Aim for a real note: a whole step (two frets higher) or a half step (one fret). The musical bends in the minor pentatonic are the 4 up to the 5, the ♭7 up to the root, and the ♭3 up a half step to the major 3rd. Push with three fingers, not one, and check your target by playing the fretted note first.
## Release, slides, hammer-ons and pull-offs
- Release: let a bent note back down without picking again.
- Slide: pick one note and slide to another on the same string, often to change box.
- Hammer-on and pull-off: sound a second note with the fretting hand alone. Smoother and faster than picking every note.
## Vibrato
Vibrato is a small, steady bend and release, repeated. Add it to long notes, especially the last note of a phrase. Wide and slow sounds like B.B. King; narrow and fast is more nervous.
## Call and response

Blues is a conversation. Play a short phrase (the call), leave space, and then answer it with a phrase that ends on a root. Repeat a good phrase instead of always playing new ones: the 12-bar form itself repeats its first line in bars 1-4 and 5-8.
## Learn licks
The Licks tab has phrases in notation, tab and on the neck. Learn one, play it in every key, then change its rhythm and its last note. A lick you can vary is worth ten you can only copy.

lessons.title: Major pentatonic and mixing it with minor
lessons.summary: The sweeter side of the blues, and how to move between major and minor.
body: ## Five other notes
The major pentatonic is 1, 2, 3, 5, 6. In A: A B C♯ E F♯. It is the major scale without the 4th and 7th, and it sounds happy, country and sweet.
## The same shapes

A major pentatonic has the same notes as F♯ minor pentatonic, its relative minor, three frets lower. So box 1 played three frets down from the A minor box (with your index finger at fret 2) is A major pentatonic. You already know the shapes; only the root moves.
## Mixing major and minor

Over the I chord, which has a major 3rd, the major pentatonic fits perfectly. Over the IV it gets risky (its 3rd clashes with the ♭7 of the IV chord). A very common approach: major pentatonic over the I, minor pentatonic over the IV and V, and the ♭3 bent up towards the 3 to slide between them.
## Listen for it
Major pentatonic phrases sound like they are smiling; minor pentatonic phrases sound like they are complaining. Most great blues players move between the two inside one solo.

exercises.title: Degrees in the major pentatonic boxes

lessons.title: Chord tones and Mixolydian
lessons.summary: Follow the changes: aim for the 3rd and 7th of each chord.
body: ## Playing the changes

The pentatonic scale fits the whole blues, but it ignores the chords. Strong players also follow the chords: they land on a note of the chord that is playing, at the moment it starts. That is called playing the changes, and it is the main skill Gleason's book builds.
## The 3rd and the 7th

The root and 5th of a chord are fine but bland. The 3rd and the 7th are the notes that tell the ear which chord it is. In A: over A7 aim for C♯ (the 3) and G (the ♭7); over D7, F♯ and C; over E7, G♯ and D.

Notice that G, the ♭7 of A7, moves only a half step to F♯, the 3 of D7. Moving by the smallest step from one chord's 3rd or 7th to the next chord's is called a guide-tone line. It makes a solo sound like it knows where it is going.
## Mixolydian

The scale that contains all the notes of a dominant 7th chord is Mixolydian: a major scale with a ♭7, 1 2 3 4 5 6 ♭7. A Mixolydian is A B C♯ D E F♯ G, the notes of D major starting on A. Over each chord of a blues you can play that chord's own Mixolydian: A Mixolydian over A7, D Mixolydian over D7, E Mixolydian over E7.
## How to practise
Play a backing track and only play the 3rd of each chord, on beat 1 of every bar. Then the 7th. Then join them with a few pentatonic notes in between.

exercises.title: Chord tones of I, IV and V
Spell all 7th chords of the blues

lessons.title: Quick change, minor blues and jazz blues
lessons.summary: Three common variations of the 12 bars.
body: ## Quick change
Go to the IV in bar 2 and back to the I in bar 3: I IV I I | IV IV I I | V IV I V. It breaks up the four long bars of the I and is used in many Chicago blues.
## Minor blues

All chords minor except the V: Im7 for bars 1-4, IVm7 in bars 5-6, back to Im7, then ♭VI7 to V7 in bars 9-10 and Im7 to finish. In A minor: Am7, Dm7, F7, E7. Use the minor pentatonic or natural minor, and the ♭VI to V7 move is the dramatic moment.
## Jazz blues

Jazz players keep the 12-bar outline but add more chords: a II-V into the IV in bar 4, a diminished chord in bar 6, the VI7 in bar 8 leading to a II-V in bars 9-10, and a turnaround in bars 11-12. In F: F7 B♭7 F7 Cm7-F7 | B♭7 B°7 F7 D7 | Gm7 C7 F7-D7 Gm7-C7.
This is exactly the harmony Gleason's book works with, so you will meet the jazz blues again in Level 4. For now, hear how the chords move and try targeting the 3rd of each one.

exercises.title: Chord tones of the minor blues
